# **Motivation**

***

This case study explores working with spatially-informed gene expression data, also known as {{< glossary "Spatial Transcriptomics" display="Spatial Transcriptomics (ST)" >}}, to explore {{< glossary "Differential Gene Expression" display="differential gene expression" >}}.

:::{.definition_box}
::::{.definition_box_header}
Differential Gene Expression
::::
::::{.inner_block}
The difference in expression of a gene between samples or cases. Differential expression is typically thought of as a difference in abundance or amount of expression, but may also be a difference in what cell types a gene is expressed in or where a gene is expressed spatially within a tissue.
::::
:::

Spatial Transcriptomic methods produce data that allow for gene expression to be investigated and described within a spatial context. 

:::{.definition_box}
::::{.definition_box_header}
Spatial Transcriptomics
::::
::::{.inner_block}
Spatial Transcriptomics (ST) refers to molecular methods used to measure gene expression at or near single-cell resolution, reporting where observed transcripts are physically located within the source tissue, preserving spatial context.
::::
:::

In this way, researchers can explore where a gene is expressed within a tissue and how that may change over time, based on experimental conditions, or for different clinical contexts. Spatial transcriptomics is a rapidly-evolving area of development that can be used for {{< glossary "Hypothesis generation" display = "hypothesis generation" >}} for a variety of biological questions such as describing cell neighborhoods, cell-cell interactions, and discovering biomarkers or drug targets. 



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html//1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk_h51840eb841718f1d_6_7.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Illustration showing the uses of spatial transcriptomics, underlining that it is largely used to generate hypotheses, desciribing cell neighborhoods and cell interactions as well as discovering biomarkers or niche interface processes. It can complement results from single cell RNA seq and be integrated with images for deeper understanding.' width=100%}
:::
:::


Platforms or technologies to generate spatial transcriptomics (ST) data are typically categorized as either {{< glossary "Sequencing-based technologies" display="sequencing-based" >}} or {{< glossary "Image-based technologies" display="image-based" >}}. Both types will provide researchers with spatially-informed gene expression data, however one type allows researchers to investigate the whole transcriptome while the other is limited to a specified set of genes called a {{< glossary Panel display=panel >}}. Inversely, the ones that investigate the whole {{< glossary Transcriptome display=transcriptome >}} typically have to deconvolve {{< glossary Multicellular display=multicellular >}} {{< glossary Spot display=spots >}} to estimate single-cell data while the ones that investigate a limited set of genes have a single-cell or sub-cellular view of expression and instead must segment the data into discrete single cells [@Lim_Wang_Buzdin_Li_2025]. Often researchers will use complementary spatial transcriptomic approaches. For example, @Kwon_etal_2026, first used a sequencing-based approach and used the results to design an image-based approach. They then used the results together to study the impact of {{< glossary Schizophrenia display ="schizophrenia (SCZ)" >}} within the {{<glossary "Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex" display="dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC)" >}} in {{< glossary "Postmortem samples" display = "postmortem brain samples" >}}. 

The technologies and their trade-offs as well as the biological concepts (e.g., SCZ and dlPFC) will be described in more detail in the [Context](https://www.opencasestudies.org/ocs-bio-spatial-transcriptomics/#context) section of the case study.

In this case study, we will use `spatialGE`, an R tool [@Ospina_Wilson_Soupir_Berglund_Smalley_Tsai_Fridley_2022], to work with image-based spatial transcriptomics data generated by @Kwon_etal_2026, specifically focusing on: 

* The data that is produced by the image-based platform.
* Importing the data.
* Inspecting and working with a `spatialGE` object that stores the data.
* Performing {{< glossary "Quality Control" display="quality control" >}} and filtering out low quality or irrelevant data.
* Transforming or normalizing the image-based data to account for technical artifacts [@Atta_Clifton_Anant_Aihara_Fan_2024].
* Creating data visualizations known as {{< glossary "Quilt plot" display="Quilt plots" >}} to visualize spatial patterns of gene expression.
* Annotating cells within the dataset, exploring cell type specific spatial patterns of gene expression.

Downstream analyses for more global and statistical summaries of spatial patterns will be introduced but not shown in-depth within this case study.

***

# **Context**

***

This section will cover context related to spatially-informed gene expression data as well as the human nervous system and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, and schizophrenia.

## What is spatially-informed gene expression data?

***

Spatially-informed gene expression data goes beyond just gene expression and reporting how much a gene is expressed in a sample or a cell. In addition to that, spatially-informed gene expression data anchors those "counts" to a physical location in the sample such that the location of cells is preserved and the contextual environment or neighborhood can also be considered. 

Spatially-informed gene expression data is also known as spatial transcriptomics or ST data. It may also be called spatially-resolved transcriptomics or SRT data by others. It is **complex**, **sparse**, and can be **noisy** (e.g., due to technical artifacts associated with image-based data). 

<details><summary> ST data vs bulk and single-cell data </summary>

Bulk RNA-seq data has very few similarities to ST data. They both provide researchers with gene expression counts. Depending on the method used for sample preparation, they both may be targeting polyadenylated tails, however for Bulk RNA-seq this would be occurring during sample preparation, while for sequencing-based ST methods, this would be occurring post sample preparation. Some ST methods don't provide high cellular resolution and may be  producing data for multicellular spots that contain 10s to 100s of cells. These methods must deconvolve the signal to separate out cells from each other; however, bulk RNA-seq is producing data for many more cells at a given time. Coverage is much higher for bulk RNA-seq than spatial transcriptomics which returns sparse, low-coverage data. 

Single-cell RNA-seq data shares some more similarities with ST data, but is still quite different since Single-cell RNA-seq data cannot preserve the spatial context. ST data can be single-cellular, but it may also be sub-cellular or multicellular depending on the technology used. But the final data product will use segmentation or deconvolution to provide single-cell like data. Both utilize (single-cell) or may utilize (ST) unique molecular identifiers (UMIs) to identify unique source molecules, and produce data that are sparse with low coverage. 

|                         | Bulk RNA-seq    | Single-Cell RNA-seq | Spatial Transcriptomics |
|:------------------------|:---------------:|:-------------------:|:-----------------------:|
| What is being processed | Pooled Cells    | Single cells dissociated from the tissue sample | Spatial spots still in the tissue. May be multicellular or near single-cellular |
| Spatial Context | Lost | Lost | Preserved |
| Cellular Resolution | None, signal is averaged | High | Variable, but high for image-based |
| Coverage | High | Lower than bulk | Low |
 
**Spatial data is the most complex of the three because it's not just reporting gene counts, but also reporting where expression of those genes were observed in relation to other genes and other areas where that gene was expressed.**

</details>

### ST technologies

The types of technology used to generate spatial transcriptomics data are generally categorized as {{< glossary "Sequence-based technologies" display = "sequencing-based" >}} or {{< glossary "Image-based technologies" display = "image-based" >}} and lie across two inverse spectra: Molecular {{< glossary Resolution >}} and Cellular Resolution. Sequencing-based technologies typically provide a whole {{< glossary Transcriptome display = "transcriptome" >}} view (broad molecular resolution), but not at a single-cell or sub-cellular resolution -- instead at a Region of Interest (ROI) or {{< glossary Spot display = '"spot"' >}} resolution (where a "spot" is made up of tens to hundreds of cells.) In other words, sequencing-based technologies provide low precision / cellular resolution. In contrast, image-based technologies typically provide data for a panel-based subset or a limited selection of the transcriptome (in other words, narrow molecular resolution). However, image-based technologies provide data at a single-cell or even sub-cellular resolution (high precision cellular resolution). Due to this, researchers may first collect spatially-informed gene expression data with a sequencing-based technology for initial hypothesis generation to identify a specific region of interest in a tissue or specific genes to probe where greater cellular resolution would be beneficial, and then follow-up with generating a higher cellular resolution spatially-informed dataset using an image-based technology. @Kwon_etal_2026 is a study posted to bioRxiv recently where the researchers did just this: first using a sequencing-based technology followed by an image-based technology as complementary spatial transcriptomic approaches to study the impacts of {{< glossary Schizophrenia display = "schizophrenia (SCZ)" >}} within the {{< glossary "laminar domains" >}}, microenvironments, and cell types of {{< glossary "Postmortem samples" display = "postmortem samples" >}} from the human {{< glossary "Dorsolateral prefrontal cortex" display="dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC)" >}}.

The molecular resolution of Visium, a sequencing-based technology is high because it gives a view of the whole transcriptome. The Molecular resolution of Xenium, an image-based technology, is low because it gives a view of a only a limited number of genes from a specified panel. On the other hand, the cellular resolution of Visium is lower than that of Xenium. Visium does not provide a single-cell resolution. Rather its spot-level resolution can have multiple cells represented. Xenium provides single-cell or even sub-cellular resolution.' width=100%}

| Technology category | Example        | Molecular Resolution | Cellular resolution  |
|:--------------------|:--------------:|:--------------------:|:--------------------:|
|Sequencing-based     | {{< glossary Visium >}}, GeoMx, Slide-seq | Broad; whole transcriptome | Low; Near single-cell but typically spots with tens to hundreds of cells represented |
|Image-based          | {{< glossary "Xenium" >}}, CosMx, MERFISH | Limited; panel of specific genes | High; single- or sub-cellular resolution |

@Lim_Wang_Buzdin_Li_2025 provides a deeper discussion comparing the various technologies available to generate Spatial Transcriptomics datasets in detail [in Table 1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s12864-025-11235-3/tables/1).

<details><summary>Broadly, how is the data generated?</summary>

#### How sequencing-based data is generated

Generally, sequencing-based methods use special slides that have spatially-barcoded RNA-binding probes attached to spots, with each spot having a unique spatial barcode. The probes also have a random molecular tag (UMI), and a polyT sequence to bind polyA tails of mRNA. Tissue is permeabilized after being placed on the slides such that mRNA molecules will diffuse through the tissue to the probes on the slide. The bound RNA is converted into cDNA with second strand synthesis on the slide, which is then extracted, library prepped, and sequenced off slide. Due to the spatial barcode, its original spatial location is preserved. Since this approach utilizes spots on a slide, these spots may align with multiple cells at a time rather than corresponding to a single cell. Different sized slide spots will have different cellular resolution. By utilizing 2 micron adjoining spots instead of 55 micron separated spots, Visium HD has finer cellular resolution and provides closer to single-cell results, however fewer UMIs and genes will be observed due to capture efficiency limitations and the smaller spot area.

@Lim_Wang_Buzdin_Li_2025 notes: 

>Platforms like Visium HD and Stereo-seq can detect only a few hundred to a thousand genes when data are exported to achieve single-cell scale/resolution. This level of resolution comes at the expense of a reduced number of detectable genes. As of now, sequencing-based spatial technologies are not yet capable of delivering whole-transcriptome data at true single-cell resolution.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html//1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk_h6ef487c1d4de554_0_0.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


#### How image-based is generated

Generally, image-based methods also use special slides, however they do not have spots or reagents attached to the slide. Instead, the slides are optimized for tissue adherence and imaging protocols. Samples are mounted to the slides and any necessary reagents for *in situ* synthesis and hybridization are applied to the entire sample section through fluidic wash channels. Probes which are specific to certain mRNA molecules are applied to the sample and hybridize to the mRNA molecules. Secondary probes with fluorophores are then applied to the sample and imaging occurs and fluorophores are cleaved or extinguished/photobleached before the cycle repeats. Rather than one fluorophore being used to represent one gene, combinations of fluorophores across imaging rounds, (an "optical barcode") represent a given gene. Therefore, gene-specific fluorescent signals are used to ascertain what genes are expressed, noting their spatial location within the sample.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html//1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk_h6ef487c1d4de554_0_7.png){fig-align='center' width=100%}
:::
:::


While image-based methods achieve single- or even sub-cellular resolution, they are assays targeting a specific, predefined gene panel, limited in the number of unique genes that can be visualized. 

</details>

### Where to find ST data

Rather than, or in addition to, generating ST data, you may be interested in finding pre-existing ST data that was generated by others and has been made publicly available. Relevant resources include:

* the [Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO)](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/)
* the Museum of Spatial Transcriptomics [@Moses_Pachter_2022]
* CROST: a Comprehensive Repository of Spatial Transcriptomics [@Wang_etal_2024]
* Company specific data repositories

#### GEO 

> GEO is an international public repository that archives and freely distributes microarray, next-generation sequencing, and other forms of high-throughput functional genomics data submitted by the research community.

[GEO records are organized](https://www-ncbi-nlm-nih-gov.fhcrc.idm.oclc.org/geo/info/overview.html) by "Platform", "Samples", and "Series". 

* A Platform record describes the technology or platform that was used to generate the data. For a study like @Kwon_etal_2026, two different Platform Records exists: one for the Visium Data and one for the Xenium data. A Sample record describes the conditions under which an individual sample was handled and the data that was generated from it. 
* A Sample Record can only refer to one Platform Record. Even though the same source donors were used to generate the Xenium data, the data for each sample originates from a different tissue section and was the result of another protocol / analysis platform besides Visium; therefore the data from the Xenium protocol will have a different Sample Record than the data from the Visium protocol, even for tissue sections from the same source donor. 
* A Series Record is used to link or group together similar samples. For @Kwon_etal_2026, two Series Records are used: one series for the results from Visium and one series for the results from Xenium. 

GEO curators can package these records into ["DataSets"](https://www-ncbi-nlm-nih-gov.fhcrc.idm.oclc.org/geo/info/overview.html) which "represent a curated collection of biologically and statistically comparable GEO Samples". [Researchers can construct queries](https://www-ncbi-nlm-nih-gov.fhcrc.idm.oclc.org/geo/info/qqtutorial.html) to search GEO Records and DataSets to find relevant data. The [advanced search](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov./gds/advanced) is especially helpful for this.

Data from GEO can be retrieved using the Bioconductor package `GEOquery` which is what we will use within the [Data Import](https://www.opencasestudies.org/ocs-bio-spatial-transcriptomics/#data-import) section of the case study.

<details><summary>Examples of this organization with samples from @Kwon_etal_2026</summary>

GSM9223468 is the Sample Record for a Xenium sample from the Br2039 Brain. #### CROST

>Repository of spatial transcriptomics. CROST encompasses high-quality samples and houses 182 spatial transcriptomic datasets from diverse species, organs, and diseases, comprising 1033 sub-datasets and 48 043 tumor-related spatially variable genes (SVGs). ### Spatial patterns of expression

Spatially-informed gene expression data is useful for investigating **differential expression** in multiple contexts: overall transcript abundance, cell-type specific expression, and spatial distribution of expression. The spatial distribution of expression can be visually inspected using quilt plots and more thoroughly investigated using statistical concepts and models. We will discuss some of these downstream uses for exploring spatial patterns of expression.


#### Differential expression: abundance

When looking at changes in abundance, researchers are comparing gene expression between different time points, different cell types, different cases/conditions (e.g., case and control), etc., specifically looking to see if a gene is upregulated (expressed more) or downregulated (expressed less) in one compared to the other. Statistical models, such as linear or negative binomial, support this type of an analysis when it's done globally for a whole transcriptome, and the results are visualized using {{< glossary "Volcano plot" display="Volcano plots" >}}.

Typically Volcano plots are used to display the results of differential gene expression analyses for bulk and single-cell RNAseq. They may also be used for spatial transcriptomics, but are more likely to be used with sequencing-based data than image-based data since image-based methods investigate fewer genes and those genes may have been identified as potentially interesting through previous analyses. For image-based data, other methods will likely be used to show differences in abundance.


The volcano plot is a scatter plot, representing numerical data on both the x- and y-axes. The x-axis of a volcano plot is used to represent the magnitude or amount of change in the expression of a gene. The y-axis is used to represent the statistical significance associated with that change. Because so many genes are being tested, a multiple-hypothesis testing correction should be utilized (e.g., False Discovery Rate or FDR). If a gene shows a magnitude of change greater than a specified cutoff and statistical significance, the points are colored to reflect that they are differentially expressed.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html//1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk_h5d1240d022ec01ab_0_14.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Example volcano plot.' width=100%}
:::
:::


#### Differential expression: cell type

While volcano plots could be used to visualize the change in expression of genes for a given cell type between different conditions, more likely a violin plot will be used, especially if visualizing the expression of one or only a few genes rather than the whole transcriptome. 

Researchers may plot the distribution of the expression of a gene from all cells that have been annotated as a specific cell type in one condition, comparing that to a second distribution of the expression of the same gene from all cells that have been annotated as the same specific cell type in another condition.

Violin plots are not necessarily plotting the results of a statistical test in the same way that volcano plots inherently are. However, you can perform a statistical test, comparing the means of the distributions, and then annotate the violin plot with the result.

Beyond cell-type specific expression, certain biological contexts may also notice a difference in the cell type composition of a tissue. In single-cell analyses, cell types will be annotated using the expression of cell-type marker genes. If a marker gene isn't observed or is observed far less frequently in a population of cells, excluding this being for a technical reason, this could point to a change in cell composition between conditions.

#### Differential expression: spatial distribution

**Quilt plots** are the face of spatial transcriptomics. Quilt plots are a version of [a heatmap](https://hutchdatascience.org/DataViz_Considerations/04_graph_info.html#heatmaps), displaying data using color. In addition to using color as a primary means to display data, heatmaps generally are two-dimensional. More specifically heatmaps use a grid or matrix with rows and columns, though they are sometimes used to display data with non-grids that are still two-dimensional like [maps](https://www.data-to-viz.com/graph/choropleth.html). However, these are more commonly called [choropleths](https://www.standardco.de/notes/heatmaps-vs-choropleths). Plotting the gene expression using color, mapping it to a physical, coordinate-based space shares the same intent as a choropleth.

Quilt plots are primarily used to visualize the expression of a specific gene showing how much it is expressed and where it is expressed. In this case (visualizing continuous numerical data), the legend will be a color gradient bar or color ramp. 


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html//1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk_h7553ddbe789f499c_0_26.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Example quilt plot showing expression' width=100%}
:::
:::


However, quilt plots can also be used to plot more discrete or categorical data like cell annotations: spatial domain, cell type, number of expressed genes, discarded vs. kept following quality control.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html//1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk_h7351b989150c1327_35_20.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Example showing cell type with a quilt plot' width=100%}

## The human nervous system

***

The human nervous system allows humans to receive, process, and communicate signals based on input from their surroundings. The nervous system is made up of the central nervous system (CNS) and the peripheral nervous system (PNS). The CNS consists of the brain and spinal cord which direct the understanding and communication of received signals to the rest of the nervous system[@Coon_Mitterer_2015].

Neurons are a specialized cell type necessary for the communication of these signals within the nervous system and they are cells with an abnormal shape. The body of the cell has the nucleus with branch-like extensions called dendrites which receive signals. Each neuron also has slender projection off of the body of cell called an axon which transmits signals to other cells. The axon has a insulating layer called a myelin sheath to help with signal transduction. Nerves within the nervous system are made up of bundles of axons from multiple neurons[@Coon_Mitterer_2015].

### What is the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex?

***

The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) is a specific part of the frontal lobe of the cerebral cortex of the brain. The cerebral cortex is the outer layer in the upper part of the brain where cognition is localized. It's a twisted and folded structure made up of gray matter (spongy tissue made up mostly of the neuronal cell bodies) which sits atop white matter (made up of the neuronal axons and oligodendrocytes). The prefrontal cortex is also known as the "prefrontal area" and is found in the front and top of the frontal lobe. The dorsolateral portion of the prefrontal cortex is towards the top and side of the prefrontal cortex. The dlPFC roughly corresponds with Brodmann area 46 (BA46) and is involved in executive functioning and cognitive control, contributing to working memory and emotional regulation [@Kirby_etal_2024].

## What is schizophrenia?

***

Schizophrenia is a chronic neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by a spectrum of symptoms impacting a person's thoughts, emotions, and behavior [@NIMH_schizophrenia, @Coon_Mitterer_2015]. Schizophrenia symptoms are typically first observed in late adolescence [@Leucht_etal_2025]. Symptoms are generally classified as positive, negative, or cognitive [@Noble_2026; @Leucht_etal_2025]. Positive symptoms refer to mental phenomena that are added experiences beyond a usual experience such as hearing voices or experiencing hallucinations. In contrast, negative symptoms refer to behaviors or emotions that are not present in people with schizophrenia such as withdrawal / social isolation. Cognitive symptoms include attention issues, working and/or verbal memory problems, misunderstandings of social situations, and trouble with critical thinking, adaptation, planning, or problem solving. Cognitive symptoms are related to executive functioning. 

The dlPFC has been implicated as an area of interest in schizophrenia research, in part due to the overlap in behaviors associated with that region and with cognitive symptoms, but also due to research. Experimental therapies targeting the dlPFC have been found to improve executive function and working memory [@Leucht_etal_2025].


### Why collect samples from the dlPFC?

***

Given that the dlPFC has been implicated in cases of schizophrenia, specifically cognitive symptoms, researchers commonly study this area of the brain for schizophrenia research. Brain imaging studies *in vivo* (MRI, PET, etc.) do not need to collect samples because such imaging can be done with research participants [@Keshavan_etal_2020]. To study the molecular biochemistry and omics of this brain region on a larger scale than is possible with live imaging, however, postmortem samples need to be collected.


## Why is spatially-informed gene expression data used?

***

The dlPFC has several laminar domains or layers, each of which seems to have its own structure and molecular signature (e.g., cell composition, gene expression patterns, morphology, connectivity, etc.), and therefore, likely, a unique role in cognitive function. Originally introduced in the early 1900s [@Zilles_2018], these layers have been confirmed throughout the years with recent single cell and spatial transcriptomics studies using a data-driven approach in describing them rather than manually annotating them [@Maynard_etal_2021; @Huuki-Myers_etal_2024].


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html//1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk_h46301d28624b2de3_0_49.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Diagram showing the laminar domains within a slice of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.' width=480}
:::
:::


Given this, spatially-informed gene expression data is beneficial not just for studying how gene expression may differ in abundance between neurotypical cases and cases with diagnosed schizophrenia, and not just for querying if cell types show differences in expression or composition between cases, but also to query if there might be differences among these layers, a point discussed by @Maynard_etal_2021. In this way, spatial transcriptomics acts as a hypothesis generation tool either to find candidate patterns that can be assayed further or for initial investigation into mechanisms to interpret previously identified risk genes.

## Data generation

***

Xenium is an image-based spatial transcriptomics platform. Tissue samples are either fresh frozen (FF) or formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE). Each of these options has its own specific protocols necessary for further sample preparation. The machine that is used to generate data is called the "Xenium Onboard Analyzer".

### Gene panel

[Gene panels](https://www.10xgenomics.com/platforms/xenium/panels) may be read-to-use, pre-designed panels, or (usually for more cost) custom RNA panels that focus on a researcher's specific genes and species of interest.

In the design process, each gene in the panel has a codeword or optical barcode assigned to it that will be the result of probe hybridization and necessary for the eventual decoding of the observed optical signature of what is hybridizing to a transcript into the assignment of gene identity.

:::{.definition_box}
::::{.definition_box_header}
Codeword
::::
::::{.inner_block}
A distinct sequence or pattern of fluorescent signals, observed across multiple imaging cycles and wavelength channels, that represent a specific target gene. Also known as an "optical barcode".
::::
:::

The collection of unique / possible codewords for a given gene panel is called the codebook. In the codebook, the optical signatures and the gene they represent are recorded.

### Xenium Analyzer steps

For a thorough discussion of the Xenium process, consider @Lim_Wang_Buzdin_Li_2025 or [10X Genomics overview of the Xenium algorithms used by the Xenium Onboard Analyzer](https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/xenium-onboard-analysis/latest/algorithms-overview/xoa-algorithms).

#### RNA imaging

Imaging is performed in cycles: Probes which are specific to certain mRNA molecules are applied to the sample and hybridize to the mRNA molecules. Secondary probes with fluorophores are then applied to the sample and imaging occurs and fluorophores are cleaved or extinguished/photobleached before the cycle repeats. Rather than one fluorophore being used to represent one gene, permutations of fluorophores across imaging rounds, (an "optical barcode" or "codeword") represent a given gene. Therefore, gene-specific fluorescent signals are used to ascertain what genes are expressed, noting their spatial location within the sample. Images are also captured to visualize where DAPI (a proxy for cell nuclei) or cell boundary marker stains are within the sample.


#### Signal decoding

Following image procurement, RNA molecule signals are identified and filtered to remove background or low quality signal [as described by 10X Genomics](https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/xenium-onboard-analysis/latest/algorithms-overview/image-processing). The codebook is used to map the observed optical barcode from probes hybridizing to the RNA molecules to the gene it represents.

#### Nuclear and cell segmentation

Cell segmentation for v1 utilizes DAPI to stain for cell nuclei. After acquiring a DAPI image of the sample, nuclei are segmented to approximate nuclei boundaries. Then an isotropic nuclear expansion algorithm is used to approximate the cell boundaries. An alternative approach (not used for @Kwon_etal_2026) utilizes multiple stains for cell boundaries and segments using those stains rather than expanding the nucleus. 

#### Assignment and quantification

After Signal Decoding and Nuclear and Cell Segmentation have occurred, transcripts can be assigned to cells, Xenium's quality control can be run, and output files can be generated.

#### Xenium quality control

Xenium assigns each decoded transcript a Phred-style quality score, signifying a confidence level in that transcript's identity. [Control probes and codewords](https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/xenium-onboard-analysis/1.9/algorithms-overview/xoa-algorithms#qvs) are necessary for computing these quality scores.

* **Negative control codewords**

> codewords in the codebook that do not have any probes matching that code. They are chosen to meet the same requirements as regular codewords and can be used to assess the specificity of the decoding algorithm.

This means that a negative control codeword is an optical signature that wouldn't be expected to be observed in the data because the underlying probes necessary for seeing this specific signal don't match the probes that were used for any genes. If a negative control codeword is observed, it would be a false positive.

:::{.definition_box}
::::{.definition_box_header}
Specificity
::::
::::{.inner_block}
Measures a model or process's ability to correctly identify true negative cases, avoiding false positives. Also known as the True Negative Rate. Specificity or sensitivity (true positive rate) can be prioritized; specificity should be prioritized if false positives are important to avoid.
::::
:::

* **Negative control probes** 

> probes that exist in the panels but target non-biological sequences. They can be used to assess the specificity of the assay.

This means that a negative control probe is a probe that isn't expected to hybridize to transcripts within the sample. If they hybridize and are visualized, the specificity of the assay is low because.

* **Unassigned codewords** 

> unused codewords. There is no probe in a particular gene panel that will generate the codeword.

This explanation may seem like it overlaps with the "negative control codeword" definition above, and it does seem to in a way. However, this means that an unassigned codeword is an optical signature that wouldn't be expected to be observed in the data, not by purposeful design (like is the case with negative control codewords) but instead as a byproduct. There are a set number of imaging cycles, a set number of imaging wavelength channels, and a set number of fluorophores. A limited set of permutations of these signals (optical barcodes) are theoretically possible. However, not all of them are assigned to genes in the panel. Some are assigned to negative control codewords, but all of the rest are unassigned codewords.

Xenium's process for assessing the [quality of decoding is explained in this documentation](https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/xenium-onboard-analysis/1.9/algorithms-overview/xoa-algorithms#qvs), but highlights are included here:


* First to find raw quality scores: which codeword best explains the observed fluorescent signals/data for that transcript? What's the likelihood of observing that codeword compared to others?
* Bin all raw quality scores and find the proportion of negative control codewords in each bin, using this to calibrate the raw quality scores.
* Xenium uses the calibrated quality score to filter the cell-feature matrix to include transcripts that only have a quality score above a certain threshold (quality scores greater than or equal to 20). If a transcript is dropped during this process, the count that it would add to the gene isn't added to the final cell feature matrix.
* These control codewords and probes are still included in the cell feature matrix that is returned to the researcher.


#### Secondary analyses (optional)

The Xenium OnBoard Analyzer can be used to perform some secondary or downstream analyses. They are [explained in greater detail by Xenium in this documentation](https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/xenium-onboard-analysis/latest/algorithms-overview/gex-secondary-analysis-algorithms). Possibilities include:

* Filtering (removing any cells with fewer than five transcripts). Note that this filtering is applied prior to creating secondary analysis results, but is not applied to the data outputs returned to users (e.g., the cell feature matrix) outside of secondary analysis results.
* Dimensionality reduction (PCA, UMAP)
* Clustering (Graph-based or K-means)
* Differential Gene Expression

## Summary

***

:::{.emphasis_block}

In summary, Xenium technology utilizes a panel of gene-specific probes to assay the spatially-resolved expression for a targeted set of genes at a single-cell or sub-cellular resolution within tissue samples. Samples for Xenium analysis are prepared from either fresh frozen (FF) or formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue blocks. While preparation protocols differ by sample type (e.g, FF or FFPE), generally tissue sections are taken from the tissue block, mounted on specialized slides, and undergo chemical treatments for fixation, permeabilization, probe hybridization, and staining. Following sample preparation, imaging cycles are performed using a Xenium Analyzer. The Xenium Analyzer's onboard software performs nuclear and cellular segmentation to approximate boundaries between cells and assign observed transcripts to individual cells. Xenium platforms use automated real-time quality control to remove noise and lower quality data. Researchers receive a variety of data including data that reports on the localization of cells, nuclei, and transcripts, observed counts for the genes, and morphology images for the tissue sample sections.

In this case study, we will use the tool `spatialGE` to work with Xenium data from @Kwon_etal_2026. Though @Kwon_etal_2026 first collected Visium data (that ultimately informed the design of the gene panel), we will only be considering the Xenium data in this case study, especially focusing on the early steps of data processing such as data import, quality control, and normalization as well as the visualization of spatial patterns with Quilt plots.

:::

## Data context

***

The data used in this case study are from @Kwon_etal_2026 which collected dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) samples postmortem from neurotypical donors and donors with diagnosed schizophrenia. Samples were fresh frozen following collection prior to spatial transcriptomics dataset generation. @Kwon_etal_2026 generated data using both the Visium and Xenium platforms, using analysis of the Visium data to inform what Xenium data to collect. Visium data was generated for all donors as explained in [Supplementary Table 1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/biorxiv/early/2026/05/23/2026.02.16.706214/DC2/embed/media-2.xlsx?download=true) while Xenium data was generated for a subset of these donors. For donors where both Visium and Xenium datasets were generated, the tissue samples originated from the same fresh frozen tissue block or source for each donor, but the samples themselves (used to generate the data for each platform) are from adjacent tissue sections of each block. Since each platform requires its own slide mounting and chemical reagents, typically serial tissue sectioning is used to yield adjacent / comparable tissue samples that can be used for multiple experiments with different technologies.

Postmortem tissue samples from 24 donors were used to generate Xenium data. Twelve of those donors had been diagnosed with schizophrenia (denoted by **SCZ** within the study and this case study) while the other 12 were neurotypical (denoted by *NTC* within the study and **CTRL** within this case study).

The sample metadata file that we will be working with combines the metadata from [Supplementary Table 1](https://www.biorxiv.org/content/biorxiv/early/2026/05/23/2026.02.16.706214/DC2/embed/media-2.xlsx?download=true) with the GEO accession number for each sample. <details><summary> Expansion of metadata from Supplementary Table 1</summary>

We previously created a file for the Xenium samples which maps each sample's GEO Accession Number to the Brain Number ID (`geo_to_spatial_samples.csv`) and united this with the data from Supplementary Table 1 because we will need the GEO accession number in order to fetch the spatial coordinates and mRNA counts for each sample. However, the sample metadata file provided in the supplementary table only includes the Brain Number ID (`Br####`). 

The files for this project follow the naming pattern of `{sample specific GEO accession number}_{sample Brain Number ID}-{file type specific pattern}`,                       

* Listed files from GEO accession number GSE307404 (all Xenium data from this project) with `list.files()` function for one of the file types.
* Used `stringr::str_replace()` function to the specific pattern for that file type with an empty string (`""`), removing all but the GEO accession number and Brain Number ID (separated by an underscore) for each sample.
* Used `strsplit("_")` function to separate the GEO accession number and Brain Number ID for each string.
* Used `do.call(rbind.data.frame, .)` to create a data frame with the sample GEO accession numbers in the first column and their associated Brain Number IDs in the second column.
* Set the column names.
* Saved to a `.csv` file.

Alternatively, we could create this map using the `title` and `geo_accession` columns from the `pData(gse[[1]])` output we saw earlier.

</details>

The combined data from Supplementary Table 1 and the GEO to Brain Number ID map is contained in the file `spatial_samples.csv`. The `spatial_samples.csv` file is a file with a header (column names) where values are separated by a comma (`.csv`). The contents of each column are explained in the following table:

| Variable | Details |
|:-----------:|:-----------:|
| `BrainNumberID` | An identifier representing which donor brain the sample originates from. Follows the pattern "Br####" |
| `Race`          | Demographic information about donors. All samples are "CAUC" for Caucasian. |
| `Sex`           | Demographic information about donors. "M" for male or "F" for female. |
| `Age`           | Demographic information about donors. Number / decimal representing age of donor in years. |
| `RIN`           | RNA Integrity Number. Number / decimal representing the quality of the fresh frozen block tissue samples. Typically reported in hours, but could be reported in days or another measurement of time. To promote greater fresh frozen block tissue quality, generally it is recommended to [minimize the postmortem interval](https://cdn.10xgenomics.com/image/upload/v1726523282/support-documents/CG000763_VisiumHDFFTissuePrepHandbook_RevA_1.pdf) |

| `GEO`           | The GEO accession number for samples with Xenium data. NA for samples with only Visium data. |

* The `Xenium` and `GEO` variables will be used to select a subset of samples of fetch the data for those samples from GEO. 
* The `BrainNumberID` and `PrimaryDx` variables will be used to create informative sample IDs so that we can more easily observe the case (e.g., CTRL or SCZ) of samples throughout our analysis.
 
### Spatial coordinates

Classically, `-cells.parquet` files are used to store the spatial coordinates of the cells, specifically the {{< glossary Centroid display=centroid >}} locations (or centers of the cells).

The `.parquet` file type is a departure from the normal way we would expect data to be stored. Often our file types (e.g., `.csv`) store data row by row with each row containing a complete record or set of related information about a specific sample, timepoint, etc. Instead, `.parquet` files store data column-by-column. This leads to more efficient storage and querying of large data files.

This is a somewhat long but helpful video explaining the `.parquet` file type.


{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2mQ4kc9J9uQ >}}



</details>

Additional information provided in this file is [described by 10X genomics](https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/xenium-onboard-analysis/latest/analysis/xoa-output-understanding-outputs#cell-summary).

<details><summary>If `-cells.parquet` files are not available</summary>

Sometimes when you are using publicly available data rather than generating new datasets yourself, files that you may expect are not deposited or archived. 

If `.parquet` files are not available, first check if `cells.csv.gz` is available as this is an alternate format of the typical file. If not, you can use a different Xenium output to calculate the centroids typically stored in the `cells.parquet` files. This will be explored further within a click to expand section in the [Data Import](https://www.opencasestudies.org/ocs-bio-spatial-transcriptomics/#data-import) section of the case study, but this alternate file type is also introduced here:

`-cell_boundaries.csv.gz` also stores spatial coordinates. Specifically these files have many rows per cell describing each vertex that is part of a polygon, where the polygon edges represent the borders of the cell. We can find the centroid of each cell by considering all of these polygon coordinates together. The contents of this file are the result of the nucleus segmentation algorithm that expands the nuclei DAPI-stained boundaries to determine cell boundaries.

| Variable | Details |
| :-------: | :----------------------:|
| `cell_id` | A cell ID corresponding to the `barcode` variable in the mRNA counts data. Multiple rows will have the same `cell_id` value in these files. |
| `vertex_x`| The x-coordinate of a vertex between two of the edges of the polygon representing that cell. |
| `vertex_y`| The corresponding y-coordinate of that vertex between two of the edges of the polygon representing that cell. |

### General note on variety of Xenium outputs

Xenium produces a [variety of output files](https://www.10xgenomics.com/support/software/xenium-onboard-analysis/latest/analysis/xoa-output-at-a-glance). Not all of these will be shared / deposited into an archive. While some file types may be more usual or preferred by some in the field (e.g., because it's more efficient to store or it's a file type they are more comfortable with), there doesn't appear to be a specific industry standard or accepted practice on files to always use. For example, morphology images (likely stained with DAPI to mark nuclei) are often output but are not always shared. An output may be shared as a `.csv` file instead of a `.parquet` file or as a `Zarr` file instead of an `.h5` file. It may seem like you can't proceed if you don't see the file types you expect, but it's not necessarily a lost cause. Make sure that you understand:

1. What files are available and what they represent about the data. You may be able to use an alternate file type for a specific aspect of the data (e.g., spatial coordinates).
1. What file types your downstream tools expect or can work with. 
1. If you can use a file type that you have in place of a file type that you or a downstream tool usually expects, or at least wrangle it to meet your needs.
1. What (if any) specialized packages are necessary to read in and work with certain file types.

# **Limitations**
***

There are some important considerations regarding this data analysis to keep in mind:

**Limitations regarding the scope of this case study:**

This case study focuses on early steps for working with spatially-informed data produced by a Xenium Analyzer. Though the motivating reference of this case study (@Kwon_etal_2026) generated and processed both Visium and Xenium datasets, this case study only works with a subset of the Xenium data samples. In addition, though @Kwon_etal_2026 performed extensive and sophisticated analysis of spatial patterns of expression within the dorsolater prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) tissue samples, this case study primarily focuses on understanding what the data is, how to import it with `spatialGE`, how `spatialGE` stores the data, quality control, normalization, and spatial visualizations of expression for specific genes and sample-wide cell type annotations with quilt plots. More downstream analyses are briefly described within a continued learning section.

**Limitations regarding the samples and data analysis:**

The Xenium algorithm used for cell segmentation for this data, prior to the researcher receiving it, employs a nuclear expansion following DAPI staining. Given that these samples are from brain tissue and the brain has specialized cells with abnormal structure (e.g., neurons with long axon offshoots), the cell segmentation results may not truly reflect cell boundaries in the sample. At the least, this approach is unlikely to be as accurate as the approach that uses cell boundary markers in addition to DAPI staining to segment cell boundaries.

Though care was taken by @Kwon_etal_2026 to match clinical and quality demographics for their case vs control samples, demographic matching was not utilized in randomly subselecting the Xenium samples used within this case study.

@Atta_Clifton_Anant_Aihara_Fan_2024 and @Bhuva_etal_2024 argue caution against the usefulness of a few classical transformation methods, especially for image-based spatially-informed gene expression data. However, we do show the use of those methods within this case study, while introducing the cautions and an employing an alternative suggestion from @Atta_Clifton_Anant_Aihara_Fan_2024. Utilizing the tool from @Bhuva_etal_2024 is left as a continued learning exercise.

Clustering is not performed directly with the data, rather clustering from @Kwon_etal_2026 is brought over to annotate cells with matching `libname` IDs for each sample. This choice is made for a variety of reasons such as simplifying the case study and to provide learners with an example of bringing in an outside annotation which may be useful for their own work. Given that the filtering approaches are not exactly the same between the original study and this case study, some cells were retained by the case study that were filtered by the original study. In those cases, we borrow cell type assignments from nearby cells, making an assumption that cells with similar types will be located near each other. This impacts a small number of cells in the case study, but could still be a shortcoming.

# **Ethical Considerations**
***

There are some important ethical considerations when working with data relating to this case study's main questions.

**Post-mortem donors:**

Data used within this case study originate from post-mortem human donors. Similar to organ donation, research involving the recently deceased depends upon the generosity or altruism of donors. While not technically human subjects research, there are still several important ethical questions such as those relating to end-of-life decision making and respecting the deceased's legacy. 

As described by @Pentz_etal_2005 the multidisciplinary expert Consensus Panel on Research with the Recently Dead (CPRRD) crafted ethics guidelines for this type of research, falling into the following categories:

* Review and oversight
* Community involvement
* Eligibility
* Research procedures
* Consent
* Confidentiality
* Resource use and cost
* Conclusion of research (e.g., return of remains to family or disclosure of medically relevant research results)

Even with the CPRRD ethics guidelines, ethical questions persist and @Parent_etal_2024 enumerates these questions in the following way:

* Common language to describe this research
* Oversight of proposed research
* The role of clinical staff
* Duration of research
* Infection prevention and control
* Sources and timing of authorisation
* Necessary disclosure during authorisation


**Schizophrenia:**

Schizophrenia is a condition that impacts a substantial proportion of the population [@Leucht_etal_2025]. To reduce the morbidity and premature mortality associated with schizophrenia, understanding the basis for the condition and developing treatments and therapies are important avenues of research. In particular, there is a genetic component to the development of schizophrenia, and therefore genetic and precision medicine studies are useful [@Leucht_etal_2025; @Daws_2017; @Fusar-Poli_etal_2022]. Societal stigma is associated with the condition [@Dino_etal_2025; @Leucht_etal_2025] and research resources are limited [@Daws_2017], raising ethical questions about how research funds are allocated and used [@Daws_2017], how the condition is treated [@Leucht_etal_2025], how individuals with the condition are discussed [@Dino_etal_2025], and how individuals with extreme expressions of symptoms are excluded from research or otherwise expected to pause current treatments in order to participate [@Wilson_Stanley_2006]. @Leucht_etal_2025 notes that "family psychoeducation is an easily implemented intervention that has been found to improve outcomes for individuals with schizophrenia and potentially reduce stigmatizing attidues within the family." @Fusar-Poli_etal_2022 suggests an innovative precision psychiatry roadmap that "links patients, providers, clinical laboratories and researchers through the use of screening, prognostic, diagnostic, and theurapeutic clinical prediction models" in order to "account [for] each person's variability in genes, environment, and lifestyle", but notes that it has its own "ethical concerns at the individual, healthcare and whole societal level".

Another important consideration is using respectiful language to describe those impacted by the condition. According to the [National Center on Disability and Journalism Language Style Guide](https://cronkite.asu.edu/ncdj/disability-language-style-guide), person-first language (e.g., "a person with schizophrenia" or "a person diagnosed with schizophrenia") is typically preferred over identity-first descriptions. @Dino_etal_2025 found that the scientific community has shown improvement in adopting person-first language when discussing this disorder, but that there remains room for improvement. 

**Data Management:**

Researchers need to carefully study secondary data (data collected originally by others) to ensure that they understand how the data were collected and what the variables represent. Use of secondary data, especially participant-level clinical data (e.g., from patients or research participants) requires consideration about how that data was collected and shared, and the consent of participants (Sterling 2011). 

Personally Identifiable Information (PII) and Protected Health Information (PHI) need to be managed securely to safeguard patient privacy. Samples collected post-mortem do not strictly fall under the PII or PHI categories, however [health information collected before death is still safeguarded](https://hipaapath.org/blog/post-mortem-phi-the-50-year-rule-you-re-probably-violating). The privacy of the donor needs to be considered and donor information should be managed securely, especially for cases where the condition has stigma associated with it (e.g., for donors previously diagnosed with schizophrenia).

Data that are considered PII or PHI includes names, dates of birth, contact information, account or health plan numbers, IP addresses, and medical records. You can read more about PII and PHI and ethical data handling practices in [this course](https://hutchdatascience.org/Ethical_Data_Handling_for_Cancer_Research/data-privacy.html#pii-personal-identifiable-information) with broader information regarding proactive and ethical data management and sharing can be found in [this course](https://hutchdatascience.org/Proactive_Data_Management_and_Sharing/).

**Reproducibility Considerations:**

Research is reproducible when the same methods (code, script, implementation based on description, etc.) can be used on the same data or within the same experimental system by a new researcher to recapitulate the results or findings of the original researcher. Note that just because a research result is reproducible doesn’t mean that it’s correct or valid. Research can be reproducibly wrong. However, reproducibility is always an important step towards useful, valid, and generalizable scientific discovery. However, reproducibility exists on a spectrum, and making a study perfectly reproducible is not an attainable goal. Therefore, taking incremental but tangible steps to make a study more reproducible is important as discussed in [this course](https://hutchdatascience.org/Proactive_Data_Management_and_Sharing/defining-reproducibility.html#reproducibility-exists-on-a-continuum). @Kwon_etal_2026 provide access to non-sensitive data and their version-controlled analysis code -- both important steps in making a study reproducible.

## What `spatialGE` is looking for

***

`spatialGE` provides the user flexibility in how they import their data. Users can either provide file paths or they can provide named lists with each list containing data frames for each sample. To better understand the data we have and are working with, we will provide named lists of data frames for both the spatial coordinates and the mRNA/feature counts.

Each named list will use the same sample names to show which data goes with which sample. Each data frame within a given named list will have similar structure, but different underlying data points specific to that sample.

## Fetching GEO data for these samples

***

This `lapply` will loop through the samples vector and fetch the following files for each sample from GEO using the `getGEOSuppFiles()` function from the `GEOquery` package:

* `-cell_boundaries.csv.gz` for computing spatial coordinates (a side quest explored later in a click to expand section)

* `-cell_feature_matrix.h5` for mRNA counts

:::{.emphasis_block}
<details><summary>How does `lapply` or "loop"ing work?</summary>
A function like the `getGEOSuppFiles()` function from the `GEOquery` package accepts inputs and performs specified steps with that input, providing some output following those steps.

When you use a loop to call a function for a set of inputs, the loop provides each input individually to the function. For each individual input, the function performs its specified steps and produces an output. Then the loop gives the function the next input and the process is repeated until there are no more inputs to give the function.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html//1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk_h7553ddbe789f499c_0_0.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='Generally, functions use some input to perform certain steps in certain order and provide an output. When using a loop with a function, the loop provides the function multiple inputs individually. The function takes each input separately, performs the steps, and returns an output for that input. Repeat for each input until it\'s all out of inputs to use because the loop doesn\'t have any more inputs to give the function.' width=100%}
:::
:::


We'll use an example with lab pets to show this in a more concrete way.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html//1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk_h7553ddbe789f499c_0_80.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='This image shows avatars for 4 lab members and their pets. Three of pets are cats and the fourth is a dog.' width=100%}
:::
:::


We could specify a loop (that doesn't use or call a function yet), but just goes through each of the lab members who has a cat and outputs their cat's name. Outside of the loop, we could specify the dog's name for the fourth lab member who has a dog, not a cat. Because that last part is happening outside of the loop, it is only output once rather than being output every time we go through the loop. And the number of times we go through the loop relates to the number of inputs we're looping through (in this case 3 because there are 3 lab members with cats).


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html//1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk_h7553ddbe789f499c_0_70.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='This image shows a loop that goes through lab members with cats, outputting each cat\'s name. Outside of the loop, the dog\'s name for the fourth lab member is output.' width=100%}
:::
:::


We could write a function that generalizes that process, specifically reporting the lab member and who their pet is, even specifying whether that pet is a dog or a cat, after evaluating the input. Functions are especially useful in cases like this where there is a process that has related tasks with specifiable, but slightly different behavior dependent on how an input is evaluated.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html//1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk_h7553ddbe789f499c_0_106.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='This image shows a lab that evaluates whether the pet is a cat or dog and outputs the correct message that we were doing earlier with a loop given that info. Notice that we call that function for one lab member and their pet, in this case a cat. The function is useful because we have related tasks with slightly different behavior depending on the input and so we can have dry generalized code that performs the specified tasks.' width=100%}
:::
:::

::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](index_files/figure-html//1jRNbuvQSjI4cZKAOStDUFAgAoFFBp8zIICCiG-1RZLk_h7553ddbe789f499c_0_144.png){fig-align='center' fig-alt='This image shows the function being called for the lab member with the dog and what the output would be. Notice that again, we have to call the function for this one lab member and their pet.' width=100%}
:::

Notice that we have to explicitly call this function for every lab member that we want to use it for. We would have to call the function four times, one for each lab member. Generally, we want to reduce redundancy in our code, so it might make sense to use a loop to loop through our data and call the function multiple times that way.

To reduce redundancy, we could call the function with a `for` loop. Notice because of how we defined our function, the lab member with a dog is part of the `for` loop now, instead of outside of it!


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}
::: {.cell-output-display}

`lapply` is another function that provides the functionality of a loop, meant specifically to work with functions. One intricacy of `lapply` is that the output from calling the function for a set of a items is returned in a list. (That's what the `l` in `lapply` stands for: "list".) Given that we've said that we want our `spatialGE` inputs to be in named lists, `lapply` will be helpful for us in constructing those inputs down the line.

::: {.cell-output-display}

The output is a list, but does work for all lab members.' width=100%}
:::
:::


</details>

<details><summary>How to construct an `lapply` statement</summary>

`lapply` statements have 2 parts.

1. Some iterable object such as a list or vector. This may be:
  * a named list
  * a vector with character elements
  * a vector of indices (`1:length(some_vector)`).
2. Some function to apply for each element of the iterable object. This may be:
  * a base R function 
  * a function from a loaded package or library
  * a function you've defined elsewhere in your code


If you iterate directly over a named list, the output list from `lapply` will use the same names from the input for the corresponding output. If you instead iterate using a vector of indices, the list won't have names and you may need to name the output yourself.

For more explanation and examples of using `lapply`, consider the post @andrews2021 or the [function's documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/base/html/lapply.html).

</details>
:::

A regex pattern is used to specify which files to download (there are more available than just these 3 for each sample). 

<details><summary>Details on the regex pattern</summary>

Regex is another term for a [regular expression](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/regexps.html) that is used to match a pattern. In this case, we're matching any one of 3 patterns and asking `GEOquery` to fetch only the files that match one of these 3 patterns.
 
* The "or" like behavior of this is from the vertical pipes (`|` ) in the regex. 
* The double backslashes (`\\`) are escape characters which are used in front of special or meta characters (e.g., `.`, `*`, `-`, `+`) that may otherwise be used for specific, programmatic purposes aside from literal string matching. Using an escape character in front of the special character is necessary to make sure they are considered as literal characters within the string matching rather than any special purpose or role they may serve. If only a single backslash was used, R would evaluate and drop that backslash, passing only the "unescaped" special character to regex. Therefore we have to also escape the backslash that regex uses. R will recognize and drop the first one in its string parsing, while the second backslash will remain and be recognized by the regex parsing, escaping the special characters (a dash or period in this case).

</details>


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
lapply(1:length(samples), 
       function(x) 
       GEOquery::getGEOSuppFiles(GEO = samples[x], 
                      filter_regex = "\\-cell_boundaries|\\-cell_feature_matrix|\\.parquet", 
                      baseDir = here("data/raw")
                      )
      )
```
:::


Note: You will need about 127 M (Megabytes) or (0.127 GB / Gigabytes) available on your system to fetch and store this data using this code.

Typically, `lapply` returns outputs from calling the specified function in a list. Because we don't need to store anything in R from this function (`getGEOSuppFiles` is going to store files in our computer's file system where we tell it to instead.), we're not going to assign the output to any variables. We could use a `for` loop here instead of `lapply` and it would work just as well. However, `lapply` is a tad more efficient at looping in R than `for` loops, so we use it here for its efficiency gains rather than how it outputs the function outputs.

For each sample, we want to read in the relevant file, process it (storing the data `spatialGE` needs in a dataframe) and then storing each sample's data frame in a named list. Using `lapply` again will be a good fit for this.

Because we're working with the spatial coordinates data, our file type specific pattern will be `-cells.parquet.gz`. Notice that these files are compressed (denoted by the `.gz` file extension) and the `arrow` package (which is typically used to read and wrangle `.parquet` files), needs them to not be compressed in order to read them in.




::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
decompress_read_parquet <- function(samples_metadata, sample){
  #Build file paths
  gz_file <- here(paste0("data/raw/",
                         sample,
                         "/",
                         sample,
                         "_",
                         samples_metadata[which(samples_metadata$sampleID == sample), "brainNumID"],
                         "-cells.parquet.gz"))
  
  decompressed_file <- str_replace(gz_file, ".gz", "")

  #Decompress
  R.utils::gunzip(gz_file, destname = decompressed_file, remove = FALSE, skip = TRUE)

  #Read in
  df <- arrow::read_parquet(decompressed_file)

  #Remove the decompressed file because we no longer need it
  file.remove(decompressed_file)
  
  #Select columns of interest
  centroids <- df %>%
    dplyr::select(cell_id, x_centroid, y_centroid, cell_area)

  #reclaim some R resources
  rm(df, gz_file, decompressed_file)
  gc()

  #Return
  return(centroids)

}

names(spatial_coords) <- samples_metadata$DxID
```

Earlier we explored what the `.h5` files look like because reading in the mRNA counts from the h5 files requires that we know the names used in those files.

```{.r .cell-code}
read_rna <- function(samples_metadata, sample){

  h5file <- here(paste0("data/raw/",
                         sample,
                         "/",
                         sample,
                         "_",
                         samples_metadata[which(samples_metadata$sampleID == sample), "brainNumID"],
                        "-cell_feature_matrix.h5"))
                              

  rna_h5data <- rhdf5::h5read(h5file, name = "matrix")

  rna_mat <- Matrix::sparseMatrix(i = rna_h5data$indices,
                       p = rna_h5data$indptr,
                       x = as.integer(rna_h5data$data),
                       dims = rna_h5data$shape,
                       index1 = FALSE) %>%
      as.matrix() %>%
      as.data.frame() %>%
      `rownames<-`(rna_h5data$features$name) %>%
      `colnames<-`(rna_h5data$barcodes) %>%
      tibble::rownames_to_column("genes")

  rm(rna_h5data, h5file)
  gc()

  return(rna_mat)
}
```

<details><summary>What is this code doing?</summary>

1. We define a function that we can call with `lapply` in order to process the `.h5` files and produce a list to give to spatialGE eventually.
1. Uses a similar method to read in the data files as our previous `decompress_read_parquet()` function for the parquet files, but it 
  * doesn't need to decompress them  
  * uses `-cell_feature_matrix.h5` as the file type specific pattern.
1. We read in the corresponding cell feature matrix file using `h5read()` from the `rhdf5` package. This package requires a `name` parameter which corresponds to the name of the top list. In the [What are the data?](https://www.opencasestudies.org/ocs-bio-spatial-transcriptomics/#what-are-the-data) section of the case study, we found that name to be "matrix".
1. We build a sparse matrix, using the elements of the `.h5` file that correspond to each argument
  * i: specifies the positions or indices of the rows with non-zero values in the matrix -- `indices` from the `.h5` file.
  * p: specifies the first column with a non-zero value for each row -- `indptr` from the `.h5` file.
  * x: non-zero values for the matrix entries -- `data` from the `.h5` file.
  * dims: matrix dimensions -- `shape` from the `.h5` file.
  * index1 we set to FALSE because our values are 0-based indices meaning that we start counting indices from 0 instead of 1.
1. We expand the sparse matrix to be a dense matrix that can then be turned into a data frame.
1. We set the row names to be the feature names from the `.h5` file (`features$name`)
1. We set the column names to be the cell IDs from the `.h5` file (`barcodes`)
1. We also move the rownames to the first column and name it "genes" because [`spatialGE` looks for gene names in the first column, not as rownames, making sure they are unique.](https://github.com/FridleyLab/spatialGE/blob/849c174f2c1537dc871987dfefb68da91beb96e3/R/STList.R#L415).
1. Finally we store this data frame in our named list for that sample

## Filtering

***

### Using Control Probes and Codewords

First we create a function that we can use with `lapply` that takes the filtering thresholds that we found previously as well as each counts matrix as inputs. Notice that the thresholds are named arguments meaning they have default values set to the exact variables we were working with earlier. We don't have to specify them when we call the function because they have these default values. We find the combined expression within each cell of each of the three associated controls using column sums and identify the cell IDs where the combined expression of any one of these types of controls is greater than or equal to the 99th percentile threshold. Finally, we take a union of the identified cell IDs.

By calling this function with `lapply`, we'll have a named list (`to_remove_all`) where each sample name stores a vector of cell IDs that should be removed for that sample.

We use a `for` loop to then loop through the sample names and actually filter the cell IDs within the count matrix. Recall that the cells correspond to the columns in the count matrix. Our filter is specifically using an exclamation point (`!`) to specify that if a column name is **not** the list of cell IDs to be filtered, then keep it.

We use a `for` loop for the actual filtering because we don't want to output a list. Rather we want to overwrite the `counts` slot, doing the same filtering steps for all of the samples (just using a different set of cell IDs to keep).


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
findOverlap <- function(mat, negcp = negcontrol_probe_cutoff, negcc = negcontrol_cdwd_cutoff, ucc = unassigned_cdwd_cutoff){
    which_negcp <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "NegControlProbe"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= negcp))
    which_negcc <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "NegControlCodeword"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= negcc))
    which_ucc <- names(which(mat[startsWith(rownames(mat), "Unassigned"), ] %>% Matrix::colSums() >= ucc))

    to_remove <- union(union(which_negcp, which_negcc), which_ucc)

    return(to_remove)
}

to_remove_all <- lapply(scz_spatial@counts, findOverlap)

for (sample_name in names(to_remove_all)){
    scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]] <- scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]][,!colnames(scz_spatial@counts[[sample_name]]) %in% to_remove_all[[sample_name]]]
}
```

### Using spatialGE

The filtering that we've done, while important, isn't enough. We also need to consider the overall library size of and number of features in cells. 

:::{.definition_box}
::::{.definition_box_header}
Library size and number of features
::::
::::{.inner_block}
The **library size** is the total sum of the counts in a single cell across genes. 

The **number of features** in a cell is the count of unique genes that have a count of at least one in a given cell.

## Normalizing

Transforming the raw mRNA counts is again necessary because of technical biases. Typically if working with single cell RNAseq data or data from sequencing based spatial transcriptomics assays (e.g., Visium), normalization methods try to correct for different sequencing depths in different cells. Typical methods used include log-transformation or the `SCTransform` method. The `spatialGE` package allows users to implement either of these with their spatially-resolved gene expression data. However, both of these methods are best suited to working with sequencing-based data rather than image-based data. @Atta_Clifton_Anant_Aihara_Fan_2024 and @Bhuva_etal_2024 discuss how these traditional methods may not be appropriate for spatial transcriptomics data, especially data from image-based technologies. @Atta_Clifton_Anant_Aihara_Fan_2024 recommends using cell volume or cell area when available to normalize image-based data. @Bhuva_etal_2024 introduces a method `SpaNorm` which models library size effects while taking into account the spatial information inherent in the data. The `SpaNorm` method can't directly work with an `STlist` object from `spatialGE` without first converting it to a `SpatialExperiment` or `Seurat` object. Therefore, we won't perform normalization with `SpaNorm` within this case study. We will perform normalization with the typical methods and a cell area normalization.

Transformed counts are stored in the `tr_counts` slot and we can't store more than one set of transformed counts due to the "slot" nature of the data. Since we want to run more than one method and compare them, we will need multiple different `spatialGE` `STlist` objects. We'll duplicate two here, one that we can use with `SCTransform` and one we can use with a cell area normalization.

### Cell Area Normalization

@Atta_Clifton_Anant_Aihara_Fan_2024 recommends using cell volumes to normalize image-based data when it is available, but that cell area can be used instead. We do not have cell volumes, but we do have cell areas.

>We recommend, as first choice, cell volume normalization to account for such partial cell capture within imaged regions. Cell area may serve as a proxy where volume estimates are not available.

The `spatialGE` package does not currently support any additional normalization methods besides log-transformation and `SCTransform`. However, we can perform an alternate normalization method and store its results in our `STlist` object (`scz_spatial`), using data already present in `scz_spatial` because we brought over the `cell_area` column for each cell earlier in the [Data Import]() section of the case study. 

The cell area normalization procedure requires that:

* We find the median cell area for each sample
* Then find cell specific size factors by dividing each cell's area by the median. 
* We then scale the counts by these size factors.
* Finally, similarly to the log transformation method, we add a pseudocount of one so that there are no zeros before we use a logarithm to bring the values closer together.

This approach is used in the [OSTA book chapter for Xenium workflows](https://lmweber.org/OSTA/pages/img-workflow-xenium.html#processing) and adapts code from the [`scrapper` package](https://github.com/libscran/scrapper). 

Beyond performing and storing our cell area normalization, we'll also want to add the same further modifications to the `STlist` that `spatialGE` typically does. You might wonder -- if` those steps are not necessary for the normalization process, why are we doing them? We're going to do them because other functions from `spatialGE` may expect that information to be there. A strength of the `spatialGE` package and its web application is that later functions expect quality control and normalization steps were performed. So something that the transformation function does, we'll want to do so that later steps aren't expecting it and can't find it.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
run_area_transformation <- function(stlist_obj, sample){
    
    # find median cell area
    median_area <- median(stlist_obj@spatial_meta[[sample]]$cell_area)
    # calculate cell specific size factors based on cell area
    size_factors <- stlist_obj@spatial_meta[[sample]]$cell_area / median_area
    # transform the counts using these size factors
    norm <- t(t(stlist_obj@counts[[sample]])/size_factors)
    # add a pseudocount of one to the transformed values so there are not zeroes and use a logarithm base of 2 
    stlist_obj@tr_counts[[sample]] <- log1p(norm) / log(2)

    # find gene avgs and stdevs and store
    stlist_obj@gene_meta[[sample]] <- tibble::tibble(gene_mean=as.vector(Matrix::rowMeans(stlist_obj@tr_counts[[sample]]))) %>%
      tibble::add_column(gene_stdevs=as.vector(apply(stlist_obj@tr_counts[[sample]], 1, sd))) %>%
      add_column(gene=rownames(stlist_obj@tr_counts[[sample]]), .before=1)

    return(stlist_obj)
}

for (sample_name in names(scz_spatial_tr@counts)){
    scz_spatial_tr <- run_area_transformation(scz_spatial_tr, sample_name)
}

scz_spatial_tr@misc[["transform"]] <- "cell_area"
```
