### Gene specific summaries of expression

We can also look at summaries of the expression of a few of these genes in these cell types.


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
combine_counts_annot <- function(matannot, matcount, sample_name, gene_name){
    full_join(
        matannot[[sample_name]][,c("libname", "annot")],
        matcount[[sample_name]][gene_name, ] %>% 
            data.frame() %>% 
            rownames_to_column("libname")
    ) %>% `colnames<-`(c("libname", "annot", sample_name))
}

use_combined_data <- function(mat, gene_name, use = "violin", samples = c("Br1139SCZ", "Br5314CTRL")){
  combined_data <- bind_rows(combine_counts_annot(mat@spatial_meta, mat@tr_counts, samples[1], gene_name),
                             combine_counts_annot(mat@spatial_meta, mat@tr_counts, samples[2], gene_name)) %>%
                      pivot_longer(starts_with("Br"),
                                   values_to = "tr_counts",
                                   names_to = "sample") %>%
                      tidyr::drop_na()

  if (use == "violin"){
    return(
      combined_data %>%
        ggplot(aes(x = sample, 
               y = tr_counts, 
               fill = sample)) + 
        geom_violin() + 
        facet_wrap(~annot, scales = "free_y") + 
        theme_bw() + 
        scale_fill_viridis_d(end = 0.6) + 
        ggtitle(gene_name) +
        theme(legend.position = "bottom")
    )
  } else if (use == "summary"){
    table_length <- length(unique(combined_data$annot)) * 2
    return(
      combined_data %>%
        group_by(annot, sample) %>% 
        summarize(
              min_exp = min(tr_counts), 
              max_exp = max(tr_counts), 
              avg_exp = mean(tr_counts),
              median_exp = median(tr_counts),
              var_exp = var(tr_counts)
        ) %>% 
    print(n=table_length)
    )
  } else {
    message("No other downstream uses supported besides 'violin' and 'summary'")
  }
}
```

Several functions provided by `spatialGE` can be used for downstream analyses further exploring the spatial patterns of expression. Note that many of them require computational resources beyond a personal computer/laptop and are best run with an institutional HPC.

## Spatial differential expression

The [`STdiff` function from `spatialGE`](https://fridleylab.github.io/spatialGE/reference/STdiff.html) further supports the goal of identifying differential expression within the context of spatial distribution.

<details><summary>Description of function from `spatialGE` documentation</summary>

> The method tests for differentially expressed genes between groups of spots/cells (e.g., clusters) in a spatial transcriptomics sample. Specifically, the function tests for genes with significantly higher or lower gene expression in one group of spots/cells with respect to the rest of spots/cells in the sample. The method first runs non-spatial linear models on the genes to detect differentially expressed genes. Then spatial linear models with exponential covariance structure are fit on a subset of genes detected as differentially expressed by the non-linear models (`sp_topgenes`). If running on clusters detected via `STclust`, the user can specify the assignments using the same parameters (`w`, `k`, `deepSplit`). Otherwise, the assignments are specified by indicating one of the column names in `x@spatial_meta`. The function uses `spaMM::fitme` and is computationally expensive even on HPC environments. To run the `STdiff` using the non-spatial approach (faster), set `sp_topgenes=0`.

</details>

## Spatial enrichment of gene sets

Gene sets are a predefined collection or group of genes that have been grouped together in a set because they share some characteristic such as regulatory mechanisms, functions, or involvement in a pathway. Functions like [`STEnrich` from `spatialGE`](https://fridleylab.github.io/spatialGE/reference/STenrich.html) allow users to test whether a given gene set exhibits high expression within a localized area of the tissue. 

<details><summary>Description of function from `spatialGE` documentation</summary>

> The function performs a randomization test to assess if the sum of distances between cells/spots with high expression of a gene set is lower than the sum of distances among randomly selected cells/spots. The cells/spots are considered as having high gene set expression if the average expression of genes in a set is higher than the average expression plus `num_sds` times the standard deviation. Control over the size of regions with high expression is provided by setting the minimum number of cells/spots (`min_units`). This method is a modification of the method devised by Hunter et al. 2021 (zebrafish melanoma study).

</details>

## Spatial gradients

Tissue samples can be clustered in order to annotate cell types or domains. Functions like `STgradient` from `spatialGE` use linear models and Spearman correlation coefficients to investigate if a gene is expressed more highly in cells closer to a specific reference tissue domain than cells farther away from the reference domain. 

<details><summary>Description of function from `spatialGE` documentation</summary>

> The STgradient function fits linear models and calculates Spearman coefficients between the expression of a gene and the minimum or average distance of spots or cells to a reference tissue domain. In other words, the STgradient function can be used to investigate if a gene is expressed higher in spots/cells closer to a specific reference tissue domain, compared to spots/cells farther from the reference domain (or vice versa as indicated by the Spearman's coefficient).

</details>

## Spatial autocorrelation

Moran's I and Geary's C are global spatial autocorrelation statistics that report how a gene's expression is correlated with itself spatially. Are areas of high expression located near each other forming clusters or are they dispersed throughout the sample? Rather is there no clear pattern? Cases of positive spatial correlation have a Moran's I near 1, and, spatially, similar levels of expression are clustered together. Cases of negative spatial correlation have a statistic near -1, and spatially, dissimilar levels of expression are near each other, appearing as if levels of similar expression are dispersed throughout the sample. Cases of spatial randomness do not display dispersion, instead, there's no clear pattern. Moran's I for spatial randomness are near 0. @Ospina_Wilson_Soupir_Berglund_Smalley_Tsai_Fridley_2022 notes that negative spatial autocorrelation can also be thought of as uniform expression throughout a tissue sample. Geary's C follows a similar logic but uses a different numerical scale.

Positive spatial autocorrelation instead has clusters with areas of similar expression appearing together. Spatial randomness has has no clear pattern.' width=100%}

The goal of these statistics is to evaluate if the expression of a gene exhibit spatial autocorrelation, in other words, if the expression isn't spatially random. Therefore, with the use of these statistics comes the question whether the resulting statistic is statistically significantly far from 0. For more information regarding the use of statistical tests and simulations to assess this question, consider [this resource on Spatial Autocorrelation](https://www.paulamoraga.com/book-spatial/spatial-autocorrelation.html).

<details><summary>Description of function from `spatialGE` documentation</summary>

> The function computes global spatial autocorrelation statistics (Moran's I and/or Geary's C) for the requested genes and samples. Then computation uses the package `spdep`. The calculated statistics are stored in the STlist, which can be accessed with the `get_gene_meta` function. For visual comparative analysis, the function `compare_SThet` can be used afterwards.

</details>

`````{=html}
<tr><td>RIN</td><td>RNA Integrity Number. A measure of sample quality determined by an automated software algorithm. Found by analyzing the electrophoretic separation of RNA molecules according to size, processing the resulting signal traces (electropherograms which representing how much of RNA of different sizes is present in samples) to evaluate and rank the signal features and combinations of features according to their predictive information content. Returns a value representing the overal level of RNA degradation within a sample on a standardized 1-10 scale.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Schizophrenia</td><td>Chronic neuropsychiatric disorder characterized by a spectrum of symptoms impacting a person's thoughts, emotions, and behavior. Symptoms are generally classified as positive, negative, or cognitive.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Segmentation</td><td>Process of inferring individual cell boundaries from tissue images, nuclear or other cell surface and interior marker staining, and transcript coordinates. Some algorithms if only provided nuclear staining first segment nuclear boundaries and expand them to approximate the cell boundaries. Others use the combination of stains to first find cell boundaries. After inferring cell boundaries, observed transcripts can be assigned to cells.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Sequencing</td><td>A laboratory technique that extracts and analyzes the genetic material from a sample.  
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Sequencing-based technologies</td><td>Methods that utilize microscopic regions or spots on specialized slides to sequence intact tissues, retaining the original physical location of observed RNA molecules within a tissue sample. These methods have high molecular resolution but low cellular resolution because they sequence the whole transcriptome rather than targeting a limited set of genes. However, the spots are not necessarily single-cells and data must be deconvoluted.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Slope</td><td>Coefficient within a linear model that represents both the steepness and direction of the relationship between the independent and dependent variable.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Sparse</td><td>Term used to describe the results from a single-cell or spatial transcriptomics experiment. Typically means that an experiment is low coverage, possibly because a given cell has a limited number of molecules that are being expressed at any given time. Within a data matrix, this looks like a lot of zeros. A sparse-matrix representation, on the other hand, omits these zeros, storing only the location of and values of non-zero data (though displays of this data may include periods instead of zeros if inspected). This sparse representation is used to reduce the overall storage size needed for the data.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Spatial Transcriptomics</td><td>Spatial Transcriptomics refers to molecular methods used to measure gene expression at or near single-cell resolution, reporting where observed transcripts are physically located within the source tissue, preserving spatial context.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Specialized cell</td><td>A highly differentiated cell that serves a specific purpose within a tissue. It may have a unique structure (physical shape or size) compared to other cells. It will express specific genes that other cells may not.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Spot</td><td>Refers to the regions across a tissue section that sequencing-based methods use to capture spatially-informed data. Spots often represent 10s to 100s of cells (e.g., multicellular) rather than single-cells. Each spot has a defined set of x- and y- coordinates on the slide used to capture data, relating captured data to physical locations within the tissue.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>STlist</td><td>An S4 object that the spatialGE program uses to store spatially-informed expression data for one or multiple samples. Utilizes slots for various aspects of the data and named lists within each slot to store data specific to each sample.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Subcellular</td><td>Represents part of a cell rather than a whole, single cell.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Transcriptome</td><td>Complete collection of transcripts produced by the genome in a specific cell, tissue, or organism.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Vertex</td><td>Where the endpoints of two edges meet in a polygon.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Violin plot</td><td>A plot used to visualize distributions of numerical variables. Because they visualize the density of data across possible values of the variable, they may resemble violins. Useful for comparing the variable across different biological groups.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Visium</td><td>A popular sequencing-based technology for generating spatially-informed expression data.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Volcano plot</td><td>A scatter plot that plots data points according to the observed magnitude of change on the x-axis and the statistical significance on the y-axis. Typically one point represents one gene, and the values are found by comparing the expression of that gene across different experimental conditions or clinical cases. Points are often colored differently based on whether the gene is upregulated (over-expressed) or downregulated (under-expressed) in a specific case relative to a conrol and whether the observed change reached pre-defined thresholds for statistical significance.
</td></tr>
<tr><td>Xenium</td><td>A popular image-based technology for geenrating spatially-informed expression data.</td></tr>
</table>
`````
